name: Seladelpar

lead: Seladelpar is a prescription PPAR-delta agonist approved in the US in 2024 for primary biliary cholangitis, a chronic liver disease. Fat-loss circles follow it because PPAR-delta is the same receptor targeted by GW501516-type compounds, which are promoted for endurance, greater fat burning and leanness.

It activates PPAR-delta, which reduces bile acid synthesis in liver cells; the label says the precise mechanism in PBC is not well understood. Its trials measure liver markers and itch, not fat loss or looks.

paras: Its documented use is a once-daily prescription for adults with PBC, taken with ursodeoxycholic acid or alone if that is not tolerated. Use for body composition is discussed online but is outside its approved purpose.

Reported adverse reactions include headache, abdominal pain, nausea, abdominal distension and dizziness. The label warns about fractures, liver test abnormalities and biliary obstruction. It is available by prescription only.

angle.text: Seladelpar is an approved PPAR-delta agonist that fat-loss circles watch because PPAR-delta activation is linked to greater fat burning and a leaner body. Its approved studies concern liver disease, not body composition.

lead: Seladelpar (brand name Livdelzi in the US; research codes MBX-8025 and RWJ-800025) is an oral, selective peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPAR-delta) agonist. The US FDA approved it in August 2024 for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), together with ursodeoxycholic acid in adults with an inadequate response to it, or alone in those who cannot tolerate it.[1][2]

Its connection to how people look runs through the skin and body. In PBC trials, seladelpar lowered itch scores, which matters for people whose chronic itching leads to scratching and skin damage, and it is also discussed in fat-loss and endurance contexts because it shares a target with research compounds such as GW501516.[3][4] Its studied use remains liver disease, and no studies of appearance or body-composition outcomes were found.

The approval was accelerated, based on reduction of alkaline phosphatase (ALP); the label states that improved survival or prevention of liver decompensation has not been demonstrated.[2] The European Commission granted a conditional marketing authorisation in February 2025.[1]

paras: The approved indication is primary biliary cholangitis, an autoimmune cholestatic liver disease for which options beyond ursodeoxycholic acid have been limited.[2][3][5] It is used with ursodeoxycholic acid in adults who respond inadequately to it, or alone in those who cannot tolerate it.[1][2] Wikipedia reports a 2024 study in which it reduced pruritus and interleukin-31 in people with PBC.[1][4] The EU granted conditional marketing authorisation in February 2025, with the EMA committee opinion in December 2024, and the compound holds orphan designation there.[1] Health Canada has also issued product information.[1]

The US label lists headache, abdominal pain, nausea, abdominal distension and dizziness as the most common adverse reactions. Warnings cover fractures, liver test abnormalities and biliary obstruction. Human pregnancy data are insufficient to assess risk.[2] In the 12-month RESPONSE trial, adverse events occurred in 86.7% of seladelpar patients and 84.6% of placebo patients, with serious events in 7.0% and 6.2%.[3] In an early phase 2 study at higher doses, three participants had reversible asymptomatic grade 3 ALT increases, and the authors recommended exploring lower doses.[6]

Seladelpar activates PPAR-delta. The label says its therapeutic mechanism in PBC is not well understood; relevant activity includes reduced bile acid synthesis, which published work links to fibroblast growth factor 21 signalling and lowered CYP7A1 expression in hepatocytes.[2][7] A structural study compared how seladelpar, elafibranor and lanifibranor bind PPAR subtypes.[8]
Seladelpar is used as a lysine salt. Its formula is C21H23F3O5S, with a molar mass of about 444.5 g/mol, and its ATC code is A05AX07.[1]

Wikipedia reports that the compound was licensed from Janssen Pharmaceutica and developed under the code MBX-8025, with a 2011 study examining its lipid effects in people with dyslipidaemia.[1] Studies in diabetic obese mice reported that it reversed features of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).[9] A phase 2 trial in NASH was terminated, and a phase 2 study in primary sclerosing cholangitis was also terminated.[10][11]
The FDA granted breakthrough therapy designation and then accelerated approval in August 2024, based on ALP reduction.[1][2] The EU product name is given as Lyvdelzi.[1]

No forum or community discussion of seladelpar was found. Interest in PPAR-delta agonists in fat-loss and endurance circles centres on research compounds such as GW501516; seladelpar is a separately developed prescription drug studied for liver disease, and the approved product is prescription-only.

Phase 2 (2017): a double-blind, placebo-controlled 12-week study in PBC patients with ALP at least 1.67 times the upper limit despite ursodeoxycholic acid was stopped early after 41 were randomised. ALP fell by 53% at 50 mg and 63% at 200 mg versus 2% on placebo, and all five patients who completed 12 weeks of seladelpar had normal ALP.[6]

ENHANCE (phase 3): 265 patients were randomised to 5 mg, 10 mg or placebo. The study ended early after an erroneous safety signal in a concurrent NASH trial, so endpoints were moved from month 12 to month 3 while blinded. Composite biochemical response was 57.1% (5 mg) and 78.2% (10 mg) versus 12.5% on placebo; ALP normalised in 27.3% at 10 mg versus 0%. Pruritus scores fell by 3.14 points at 10 mg versus 1.55 on placebo, and no serious treatment-related adverse events were reported.[12]

RESPONSE (phase 3, 2024): 193 patients were randomised 2:1 in a 12-month double-blind trial; 93.8% received ursodeoxycholic acid. Biochemical response at month 12 was 61.7% with seladelpar versus 20.0% with placebo, and ALP normalised in 25.0% versus 0%. In patients with baseline itch scores of 4 or more, the mean change at month 6 was -3.2 versus -1.7 points on placebo.[3][13] Secondary analyses reported lower IL-31 and itch.[4] A trial in PBC with compensated cirrhosis is registered.[14]
No studies found of seladelpar for cosmetic, fat-loss or muscle-related goals.
